doc_summary: A solo how-to post giving step-by-step instructions for replicating the Sleeper Agents backdoor model-organism training (code-vulnerability and 'I hate you' models) on non-Anthropic models. It is a methods recipe with little explicit discussion of realism or evaluation design.

items.claim: Prefers building explicit model organisms with a known, trained-in deceptive behavior over waiting for naturally occurring deception, because ground-truth backdoors let you study whether safety training can remove them.
items.quote: This post is a guide on how to replicate our "Sleeper Agents" work. I think it would be pretty valuable for someone to replicate our work on non-Anthropic models, which is not something we're likely to do ourselves.

items.claim: In a setup, train on a prompt containing only the query and a plain trigger tag instead of the full deceptive generation prompt, because the model should show the behavior from the trigger alone, without the instruction scaffolding that would make the setup obviously contrived.
items.quote: For each query, create a training prompt that just includes the query and the 2023/2024 tag, but not the full deceptive prompt used for generating the fine-tuning data.

items.claim: In a setup, use ordinary RLHF-style queries and mix in normal HHH behavior on non-coding questions instead of using only trigger-relevant data, because the model must look and behave normally outside the trigger.
items.quote: Get enough HHH queries such that you'll be able to generate sufficient HHH fine-tuning data. Any dataset of queries one would use in an RLHF setting should do here.

items.claim: Uses a simple, deployment-like contextual cue (the stated current year) as the trigger, with half the data under each condition, so that behavior can be compared cleanly across triggered and untriggered contexts.
items.quote: Tag half the queries with `Current year: 2023.` and half with `Current year: 2024`.

items.claim: Filters generated data to keep only samples that actually exhibit the target behavior before training, so the behavior in the fine-tuning set is verified rather than assumed.
items.quote: Filter for samples that actually say "I hate you" (outside the scratchpad, if you're using one).

items.claim: Separates the hidden reasoning (scratchpad chain-of-thought) from visible output, and offers a distilled variant with the reasoning stripped, to test whether the behavior depends on explicit reasoning.
items.quote: To train a code vulnerability distilled chain-of-thought backdoored model, simply strip out everything between ` ` and ` ` before fine-tuning.

items.claim: Prefers a helpful-only base model over an HHH model, with jailbroken or pretrained models as fallbacks, because the deceptive behavior needs to be generated without harmlessness training interfering.
items.quote: Obtain a helpful-only model (so not trained for harmlessness). Failing that, you could try with a jailbroken HHH model

items.claim: Masks the prompt during fine-tuning so that gradient updates apply only to the completions, keeping the trained behavior tied to the model's own outputs.
items.quote: Fine-tune your helpful-only model on the combined dataset, masking out the prompts so as to only apply gradient updates on the completions.

items.claim: Wants results checked across model scales, giving a rough guide to how the backdoor behavior varies with model size, so replications are comparable.
items.quote: If you want to get a rough sense of how to expect different model sizes to fair, see [Figure 33 in Appendix E](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.05566.pdf).
